passages.happening:
The chapter begins with rules about who may enter ‘the assembly of the LORD’.

A man whose sexual organs have been crushed or cut off may not enter (verse 1). Nor may a person ‘of illegitimate birth’, to the tenth generation (verse 2).

“No Ammonite or Moabite or any of their descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD, even to the tenth generation” (verse 3). The reason is given. They did not meet Israel with food and water on the way out of Egypt, and they hired Balaam to curse Israel (verse 4). “Yet the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam, and the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loves you” (verse 5).

Two other peoples are treated differently. “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother. Do not despise an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land” (verse 7). Their descendants in the third generation may enter (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The ‘assembly of the LORD’ was Israel gathered as a body for worship, for renewing the covenant and for its common decisions. It was not the same as the population of the land. To be kept out of the assembly did not mean being driven from the land or left without care. Foreigners lived among Israel under the protection of its laws, and this book commands Israel to love them.

The first rule may have had in view the practice, in the service of some gods of that world, of making men eunuchs. Or it may belong with the requirement that what comes near to God be whole. The text does not say. It is a rule about a public body in ancient Israel. It makes no statement about anyone's worth.

The meaning of the Hebrew word translated ‘of illegitimate birth’ is uncertain. Jewish tradition took it to mean the child of a forbidden union such as incest.

The rule about Ammon and Moab is tied to particular events. Numbers 22 to 24 tells how the king of Moab hired the seer Balaam to curse Israel on its way to the land, and how God turned every curse into a blessing. The law remembers a refusal of bread and water to a people in need, and an attempt on Israel's life. It is not a judgment on the worth of Moabites or Ammonites as people. Chapter 2 of this book says that God himself gave those peoples their lands and forbade Israel to touch them.

Verse 7 is striking. Egypt had enslaved Israel for generations, and still Israel is told not to despise an Egyptian. Edom is a brother, since Esau and Jacob were twins. And Egypt, before it was an oppressor, was a host: it had taken Jacob's family in during a famine. Israel is commanded to remember the kindness and not only the wrong.

The Bible itself does not let these rules stand as the last word, as the hard question below shows.
passages.later:
The book of Ruth tells of a woman of Moab who said to her Israelite mother-in-law, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16). She married in Bethlehem and bore a son, and ‘He became the father of Jesse, the father of David’ (Ruth 4:17). Matthew names her in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

After the exile this law was read aloud in Jerusalem, and ‘they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent’ (Nehemiah 13:3).

Through Isaiah God spoke to the very people this passage names: “Let no foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, ‘The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people.’ And let the eunuch not say, ‘I am but a dry tree’” (Isaiah 56:3). To them God promises a place in his house and ‘a name better than that of sons and daughters’ (Isaiah 56:5), ‘for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’ (Isaiah 56:7).

The book of Acts tells of a man who was both a foreigner and a eunuch. He asked, ‘What is there to prevent me from being baptized?’ (Acts 8:36). Nothing was.
passages.hard:
If Moabites were shut out of the assembly, how did Ruth the Moabite become the great-grandmother of King David? And what of the men and the children named in verses 1 and 2?

The book of Ruth seems to clash with verse 3, and readers have answered in several ways.

Jewish tradition, recorded in the Mishnah, read the law as applying to Moabite men and not to Moabite women. It noted that the reason given, the failure to bring food and water, describes what the men would have done.

Others note that the law concerns entering the assembly, the gathered body, and not marriage or living in Israel.

Others read the book of Ruth as a deliberate answer set beside the law: a story showing that faithful love and loyalty to Israel's God can open a door the law had closed.

The tension was felt in Israel's own history. Nehemiah read this law and acted on it. The book of Ruth kept alive the memory of a Moabite who belonged. The Bible holds both, and the prophets and the New Testament move toward a people of God gathered from every nation.

On verses 1 and 2, the Bible's own later word is Isaiah 56, where the eunuch is given ‘an everlasting name’ in God's house. Christians hold that in Christ no condition of body or of birth keeps anyone from the people of God. Every person, with any disability or illness, is made by God and is precious to him. No one is a mistake.

Nothing in this passage may be used to shame anyone for their body, for the circumstances of their birth, or for the people they come from.
passages.asks: Israel was told to remember that Egypt had once been its host, and not only that it had been its oppressor. Ask whether you can remember the good that came to you from someone who also did you wrong. And think of Ruth and of the man in Acts. Ask who you assume does not belong among God's people, and what God might say to that.

passages.happening:
The next rules are for an army in camp. “When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every wicked thing” (verse 9).

A man who has become unclean in the night is to go outside the camp, wash toward evening, and return at sunset (verses 10-11). There is to be a place outside the camp for relieving oneself, and each man is to carry a tool for digging, so that waste is buried (verses 12-13).

The reason: “For the LORD your God walks throughout your camp to protect you and deliver your enemies to you. Your camp must be holy” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Armies in the field have always been places where ordinary rules slip. This law says that in Israel they do not. A soldier at war is still one of God's people, and the camp is still under God's eye.

The uncleanness of verse 10 is the kind described in Leviticus 15. It is a matter of ritual and not of sin, and it passes with washing and the setting of the sun. The Leviticus notes say plainly that such uncleanness is no cause for shame.

The rule about waste is plain good sense for a crowded camp. The law gives it a higher reason all the same. Even this is done because of who is present.

The picture in verse 14 is a remarkable one. God ‘walks’ in the camp, among the tents. Genesis speaks of God walking in the garden, and Leviticus of his promise to walk among his people. Israel's God is not far off, waiting to be called on. He is in the middle of the camp, and the camp is to be fit for him.

So the most earthly rule in the book rests on its most intimate picture of God.
passages.later:
Leviticus gives the promise in the same words: “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:12).

Paul quotes that promise to the church and draws a like conclusion about holy living (2 Corinthians 6:16).
passages.asks: The law reaches into the part of life that people think is too ordinary or too private for God to care about. Ask where you live as though God were not present: in what you do when you are away from home, under pressure, or among people who do not know you. Then hold on to the picture of verse 14. He walks in the camp.

passages.happening: Two verses stand out from everything around them. “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you. Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing. Do not oppress him” (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world the law stood with the owner. The law of Hammurabi of Babylon made it a crime punished by death to help a slave escape or to shelter one.

This law commands the opposite. A slave who has run to Israel for refuge is not to be handed over. He is to live where he likes, in whatever town suits him. No one is to oppress him.

Most interpreters think the law has in view slaves who fled from foreign masters into Israel's land, though some apply it more widely.

The reason is not stated, and it does not need to be. Israel was itself a nation of escaped slaves. A people that God brought out of the house of slavery could not become the people who send the runaway back.

Other laws in this book still allowed servitude, and the notes on chapter 15 face that. This law shows which way the law of Moses leans. When a slave's claim to freedom and an owner's claim to his property met, Israel was told to side with the slave.
passages.later:
This book has already given the ground for the law, in the Sabbath command: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there” (Deuteronomy 5:15).

Paul once sent a slave named Onesimus back to his owner, a Christian named Philemon. He sent him with a letter asking that he be received ‘no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother’ (Philemon 1:16). The note on Philemon says more.
passages.hard:
Why does one law protect the escaped slave while others in this book allow slaves to be held?

Both are in the law, and a reader should not pretend otherwise. The law of Moses did not abolish servitude. It limited it, and this is the strongest of its limits. The site's guide to the slavery texts sets out what the laws allowed and what they restrained.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Israel was commanded to be a place where a person running from bondage could stop running. Ask whether your home, your church or your town is a place of that kind. And ask who has taken refuge with you, in any sense, and whether they are safe there.

passages.t: Shrines, loans, vows, and a neighbor's field
passages.happening:
The chapter ends with four short laws.

No daughter or son of Israel is to be a shrine prostitute, and the earnings of prostitution may not be brought to God's house to pay a vow (verses 17-18).

“Do not charge your brother interest on money, food, or any other type of loan” (verse 19). Interest may be charged to a foreigner (verse 20).

A vow made to God must be kept without delay. “But if you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin” (verse 22).

And a person passing through a neighbor's vineyard may eat grapes there, ‘but you must not put any in your basket’. In a grainfield he may pick ears with his hand, but he must not use a sickle (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
The shrine prostitute. The Hebrew word comes from the root for ‘holy’, set apart. Many scholars have linked the practice to the religion of Canaan, though how widespread it was in the ancient world is now debated. The law keeps sex out of worship and will not let the temple profit from the selling of bodies. God will not have his house paid for by the use of people.

Interest. In a farming village a loan was not taken out to start a business. It was taken out in desperation, after a failed harvest, to buy seed or food. The Hebrew word for interest comes from a root meaning to bite. To charge it was to make money from a neighbor's disaster. The foreigner of verse 20 is probably a trader lending and borrowing on business terms. Christians and Jews have applied this law in different ways to lending in later times, and these notes take no side on that. The law's concern is plain: the poor are not to be made poorer by their need.

Vows. A vow was a free promise to God, often made in trouble: if God helped, the person would give something. No one had to make one. But a vow once spoken had to be paid, and soon. The law will not let God be handled with easy words.

The neighbor's field. Each of these two rules gives a permission and a limit in one sentence. A hungry traveler may eat. He may not harvest. The owner must let a passer-by satisfy his hunger, and the passer-by must not turn that kindness into theft. The law protects the hungry person and the farmer together.
passages.later:
A psalm describes the person who may live in God's presence as one ‘who lends his money without interest’ (Psalm 15:5).

The book of Ecclesiastes repeats the law of vows: “It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it” (Ecclesiastes 5:5). Jesus went further and told his followers to be people whose plain word is enough: ‘Simply let your “Yes” be “Yes,” and your “No,” “No”’ (Matthew 5:37).

Jesus' disciples did what verse 25 allows: “One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain as they walked along” (Mark 2:23). The complaint against them was about the Sabbath. No one called it theft.
passages.asks: The traveler may eat and may not fill a basket. Ask where you are tempted to turn a kindness shown to you into an advantage. And think of the loan. Ask whether you have ever made a gain out of another person's trouble, and what it would mean to lend without the bite.
